newsitem.title: ITALY: FOCUS-Italian tax rebate ups stakes in EMU gamble.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Italian tax rebate ups stakes in EMU gamble.

text.p: Italy is raising the stakes in its bid to join European economic and monetary union (EMU), promising to reward taxpayers in 1999 for putting up with a hefty dose of pain in a do-or-die "budget for Europe" next year.

But the government could be storing up problems for the future by stinging Italians with a "Eurotax" but committing to pay them back before it even knows whether a bold gamble to make the EMU high table by 1999 has come up trumps, analysts said.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi spelt out on Tuesday how the government plans to raise 12.5 trillion lire ($8.2 billion) next year through a number of measures including a once-off hike in income tax which will be partly reimbursed in 1999.
"The measures announced today are the only option for the government to sell the budget to the public," said Ken Wattret, an economist in the London office of Paribas.
The Euro-tax package, thrashed out in two days of meetings between the government and trade union leaders, has headed off the threat of a general strike.
"But I don't think they are doing such a good job of selling Italy to the rest of the European Union," Wattret added.

Some officials at the German central bank, the Bundesbank, have suggested Italy and Spain should be kept out of a currency union because they do have not built up a convincing reputation for keeping their financial affairs in good order.

The Eurotax is a key part of a 1997 budget -- which cleared the lower house of parliament at the weekend -- tailored to lop 62.5 trillion lire off the 1997 public deficit and speed Italy on its way to EMU membership by 1999.

Prodi and his economic team are pinning their hopes on Italy reaping a huge premium in the form of lower interest rates if it qualifies for EMU membership at the outset in 1999. Italy plays an enormous interest rate bill to service a national debt amounting to some 120 percent of the country's economic output.

The government wants to wrestle down the public deficit to three percent of gross domestic prodict (GDP) by the end of 1997, thereby meeting a key requirement of the Maastricht Treaty which traces out the road to EMU membership.

Prodi said 5.5 trillion lire would be raised by the one-off hike in income tax, 3.5 trillion lire by bringing forward taxes imposed on company severance payments and 2.5 trillion lire from collecting taxes that have already fallen due.
The remaining one trillion lire would come from renegotiating Italy's foreign currency debt.

Prodi told a news conference that tax-payers would be partly reimbursed for the income tax with the choice of a rebate from 1999 or options entitling holders to a discount on shares in Italian state companies due to be sold off.

"By offering to pay the money back this is screaming out loud that they are just trying to manipulate the figures to meet the three percent public deficit target," said Sally Wilkinson, an economist at UBS.
"I doubt if this rebate idea will make France and Germany very happy either," said Wilkinson. "Without the rebate the tax measure was entirely credible even though it was only once off."
The promise of a tax rebate is a sign the government was badly shaken when hundreds of thousands of Italians took to the streets 10 days ago in a huge anti-budget demonstration in Rome.

Some economists are also concerned that higher taxes next year will depress an already sluggish economy and hit tax receipts, making it even harder for the government to meet its three percent deficit-to-GDP target.
